pages.x: Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh had declared Vietnam independent of France in 1945, and fought the French for nine years. In 1954 they surrounded a French army in the valley of Dien Bien Phu and forced it to surrender. At a conference in Geneva Vietnam was split, for the time being, into a communist North and a South backed by the United States.

The elections promised for 1956 to unite the country never took place. In the South communist guerrillas, the Viet Cong, armed and led from the North along the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia, fought the government of Ngo Dinh Diem. The United States sent advisers, then thousands of troops.

In 1964 President Lyndon Johnson used a reported attack on American ships in the Gulf of Tonkin to win Congress's backing for war. In 1965 he sent in combat troops and began bombing the North. By 1968 more than half a million Americans were in Vietnam.

In January 1968, at the Tet new year festival, communist forces attacked cities across the South, even the American embassy in Saigon. They were beaten back with huge losses, but Americans had been told the war was being won, and the shock turned many against it. In March Johnson said he would not run again.

In March 1968 American soldiers killed some 500 unarmed villagers, most of them women, children and old people, at My Lai. Over Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia American planes dropped more bombs than in the whole of the Second World War, and sprayed forests with Agent Orange, a poison whose harm is still felt.

It was the first war watched on television, and at home the protests grew. Hundreds of thousands marched, young men burned their call-up papers, and in 1970 soldiers of the National Guard shot dead four students at a protest at Kent State University in Ohio. President Richard Nixon began to bring the troops home, while bombing harder.

A peace deal in 1973 let the last American troops leave. Two years later the North attacked again, and on 30 April 1975 its tanks crashed through the gates of the presidential palace in Saigon, as American helicopters lifted the last people from the rooftops. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

Vietnam was united under communist rule, and hundreds of thousands of boat people later fled by sea. In the United States the defeat left deep wounds and a distrust of government. Today the two countries trade and talk as friends, and a black granite wall in Washington carries the names of the 58,000 Americans who died.
